en: Geothermal power plants in Tiwi, Albay generate electricity by using underground steam heated by magma to spin large turbines.
The southwest monsoon picks up moisture from the West Philippine Sea, causing heavy rainfall over western Luzon.
Water flowing down the Agus River from Lake Lanao spins turbines to generate most of Mindanao's hydroelectric power.
The Philippine Trench formed when the Philippine Sea Plate collided with and slid beneath the Eurasian Plate.
Slightly acidic rainwater dissolves the limestone rock in the Tabon Caves, slowly carving out massive underground chambers over millennia.
Prolonged exposure to unusually warm ocean water causes coral polyps in Tubbataha Reef to expel their algae, turning the corals white.
Weathered volcanic ash from past Mount Pinatubo eruptions released essential minerals into the soil, making Central Luzon highly fertile for agriculture.
The dense root systems of mangroves in Olango Island trap moving sediments, which gradually builds up the shoreline and blocks storm surges.
Typhoons gain immense strength by absorbing heat and moisture from the warm surface waters of the Pacific Ocean before hitting the Philippines.
Taal Volcano's violent phreatic eruptions occur when rising hot magma directly contacts the cold water of the main crater lake, causing instant steam explosions.
The northeast monsoon brings cold, dry air from Siberia across Asia, resulting in cooler weather for the Philippines between November and February.
The tall peaks of the Sierra Madre mountain range force moist winds upward, causing heavy rain on the eastern side while keeping the western side drier.
